files.text:
On winter evenings in Rome, over the reedbeds of the Somerset Levels, at the piers of Brighton and Aberystwyth, starlings coming in to roost gather above the place where they will sleep and fly together for half an hour before they go down. The flocks run to tens of thousands of birds, sometimes far more. They do not follow a leader. Each bird watches a handful of those nearest to it and keeps with them, and the whole cloud turns, stretches into ribbons, folds over itself and pours across the sky as one thing.

In 2008 a team in Rome filmed the flocks over Termini station with synchronised cameras and rebuilt them in three dimensions, bird by bird. Each starling, they found, keeps track of six or seven neighbours whatever the distance between them, a fixed number of birds rather than a fixed radius, and that is what lets a flock stretch thin and dense again without breaking apart.

A peregrine changes everything. When a falcon dives at the flock, the birds nearest to it bank hard away, rolling almost onto their side for a quarter of a second and back again, and their neighbours copy the roll a fraction of a second later, and theirs after them. From the ground it is a band of darkness sweeping across the cloud, because a starling seen from below and to the side is a thin dark line when it flies level, and a whole wing when it banks.

Nothing here is drawn as a wave. Every bird is flown on its own, steering by its seven nearest neighbours, banking to turn as a bird must, and drawn as its own silhouette, two wings and a body, from a camera standing in the field. Click or tap the sky and a peregrine stoops through the flock there, on its own line, and is gone. The dark bands that follow it are only many birds, one after another, turning their wings toward you. Leave the sky alone for a while and the flock comes down into the copse, and the evening is as the painter left it.

# murmuration George Inness's *A Winter Sky* (1866), a frozen marsh at the end of a December afternoon, with forty thousand starlings flying in its light. The flock stretches into ribbons, folds over itself and thickens to a dark core where you look along it. Click or tap the sky and a peregrine stoops through: dark bands sweep across the flock as bird after bird rolls its wing toward you, the cloud opens round the falcon and closes behind it. Leave it alone and the flock pours down into the copse on the left, and the painting is as Inness left it. ```html
``` ```js import { murmuration } from './murmuration.js'; const destroy = murmuration(el, { birds: 5000 }); destroy.scatter(); // a falcon stoops through the flock destroy.scatter(0.6, 0.3); // ...through that point (fractions of the element) destroy.roost(); // send them down into the copse destroy.wake(); // up out of it again destroy(); // remove everything it added ``` Without JS it is the painting. Nothing is ever drawn over the painting at rest: an empty sky is the scan, pixel for pixel. ## The real thing - A murmuration is a winter roost gathering: tens of thousands of starlings (sometimes far more) flying together for up to half an hour before dark, then pouring down into reeds or trees. - Starlings fly at about 10 m/s, wingspan 37-42 cm, nearest neighbour about 0.7-1 m. The flock is a thin sheet a few birds thick, much wider than deep. - Each bird follows six or seven neighbours by rank, not by distance (Ballerini et al. 2008, the STARFLAG study over Rome). - When a peregrine attacks, birds near it make a "zig": a fast roll almost onto the side and back. Neighbours copy it after about 76 ms, and the roll sweeps through the flock as a dark band faster than any bird flies (Procaccini et al. 2011; Hemelrijk, van Zuidam and Hildenbrandt 2015). - The band is dark because a starling seen from below and to the side is a thin line in level flight and a whole wing when it banks. ## How it works **The flock.** 7,000 birds (3,000 on a phone) are flown in three dimensions, in metres and seconds, about 250 m from a camera at eye height: a long lens from the far side of the marsh, so the flock is only 7-12 degrees above the horizon and level birds are nearly edge-on. Each finds its **seven nearest neighbours by rank** every other frame with a uniform-grid spatial hash and takes from them separation (inside 2 m, stronger fore and aft than to the sides, as Ballerini measured), alignment, and cohesion weighted by how much it is on the edge (StarDisplay, Hildenbrandt, Carere and Hemelrijk 2010). Birds on the edge pull in hard, so the boundary is crisp and dense, as in real flocks. Now and then a few birds start a turn or a climb of their own and the rest pick it up through their neighbours (Attanasi et al. 2014); that is where the ribbons and folds come from. Nothing draws a shape. **Flight.** Birds turn by banking: the sideways wish becomes a roll angle, atan(a/g), and the tipped lift does the turning, so the flock swings rather than slides. Wings flap in bouts at about 12 beats a second with glides between. **Companions.** Each flown bird carries five companions that keep station on it inside its own personal space (a fixed place beside, ahead or above, with a slow drift and their own wingbeat phase). They are drawn, not flown: they share their bird's heading and roll, so they take part in every turn and every escape. This is how the sky holds 42,000 starlings (18,000 on a phone) while the CPU steers 7,000. Spacing is set so the nearest neighbour among all of them is about 0.7 m. It is a simplification and I say so: within a group of six, birds do not steer independently. **Drawing.** Each bird is one WebGL point sprite whose fragment shader draws its projected silhouette, two tapered wings and a body, with analytic coverage. A wing's thickness on screen is how much of its surface faces the camera; for a flapping bird that is taken at the stroke's mean dihedral (at 12 Hz the eye sees the average), while the wing tips still beat. Contrast falls slowly with distance (aerial perspective), so far birds take on the painting's sky. Over the bright opening the flock is near-black; over the cloud bank it all but disappears, as a real one does. **The falcon and the waves.** A click or tap sends a peregrine, about a metre across, stooping through that point on its own line at up to 34 m/s and out the other side. It never follows the pointer, and nor do the birds. Within 9 m starlings get out of its line of flight (a vacuole, a split). Within 14 m a starling zigs: it rolls 83 degrees in 0.25 s, holds 0.12 s, rolls back over 0.3 s, then will not repeat one for 2.5 s, so one attack sends one wave. Its neighbours repeat the zig after a reaction time drawn around 76 ms (SD 10 ms). The roll travels at nearest-neighbour distance over reaction time, about 15 m/s. Nothing paints the wave: it is many birds, in a row, showing you their wings. **The painting.** The plate is the 3,400 px scan, shown as a plain `` with `object-fit: cover`. Offline, `assets/bake-land.py` makes a one-channel mask of everything in front of the sky (the line traced by hand over the full scan, then refined within 40 px by the paint itself, since the crowns are darker than the cloud bank behind them). The shader multiplies each bird by one minus the mask, so birds go behind the copse; the mask is never drawn. The camera is fitted to the plate: the horizon is the far treeline (57.5% down), the flock flies in the clear opening (19-30% down) and is about 45% of the painting's width, whatever the crop, so the birds keep one size against Inness's brushwork. **The roost.** After `data-roost` idle seconds (or `roost()`) the roost point moves to the copse and the preferred height becomes a cone over it: the birds spiral in and go down behind the crowns. When they are all in, the loop stops and the painting is untouched. ## The statechart ``` flying ──HUNT──▶ hunted ──CLEAR──▶ flying │ │ └──ROOST─────────┴──▶ roosting ──SETTLED──▶ roosted │ │ └──WAKE / HUNT────────┴──▶ flying ``` Mirrored to `data-state`; a `murmuration:state` event bubbles on every transition (`detail: { state, from, event }`), so a wing sound can be hung on `hunted` later. ## Options | JS option | data attribute | default | | |---|---|---|---| | `birds` | `data-birds` | `7000` | Birds flown (each carries `group - 1` companions). | | `birdsPhone` | `data-birds-phone` | `3000` | The cap on phones. | | `group` | `data-group` | `6` | Birds drawn per bird flown (1-8). `1`: every bird is flown. | | `roost` | `data-roost` | `75` | Idle seconds before they go down; `0` never. | | `falcon` | `data-falcon` | `tap` | `none`: clicks do nothing (`scatter()` still works). | | `seed` | `data-seed` | random | The same flock every load. | | `ink` | `data-ink` | `0.86` | Opacity of a single bird. | | `mask` | `data-mask` | `assets/winter-land.png` | The land mask, if you swap the painting. | | `renderer` | `data-renderer` | `auto` | `2d` forces the Canvas 2D fallback. | | `adapt` | `data-adapt` | `on` | `off`: never retire birds on a slow device. | | `label` | `data-label` | (a sentence) | Accessible name of the picture. | Another painting: replace the ``, bake a mask with `bake-land.py`, and set the `PLATE` measurements at the top of `murmuration.js` (horizon, roost span, treetops, the clear band the flock should fly in). ## Theming | Property | Default | | |---|---|---| | `--mm-bird` | `#221c19` | The starlings and the falcon: a dark from the painting's copse. | | `--mm-aspect` | `3400 / 2476` | Shape when the element has no height of its own. | Frame the plate with `object-position` on the ``; the camera follows it. ## Accessibility and reduced motion The stage is `role="img"` with a label, and focusable: Enter or Space sends the falcon through the flock. The painting is decorative (`alt=""`). A vertical swipe scrolls the page (`touch-action: pan-y pinch-zoom`); only a tap that does not move sends the falcon. With `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` nothing moves: the flock is shown still, formed, in the sky, and clicks do nothing. ## Performance The loop runs only while the plate is on screen and the tab is visible, and stops for good once the flock has roosted (zero rAF at rest, checked). DPR is capped at 2. On a slow device, if a frame's work stays over 12 ms the flock retires a fifth of its birds at a time (they fade out) down to 40%. Neighbour search is the cost: about 4-8 ms for 7,000 birds on a laptop. ## Credits George Inness, *A Winter Sky*, 1866, Cleveland Museum of Art, Bequest of John Huntington 1927.388, CC0. The land mask is derived from it.
